name: Tomas Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Tomas, 58. I have a two-year college diploma and work as a junior developer for a tech company that sells water-bill software to utilities. I correct small meter-entry problems, then a senior checks the code because I still miss edge cases. The best part is seeing a family’s wrong bill put right. I have never used AI tools; I work through the meter record and the test sheet myself.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mira works regular hours at a community library, and our children are grown. My pay is typical for this job, we have a mortgage, and about four months of expenses saved. There are some other developer jobs nearby, though I would need to show I can do more than junior fixes. We talk about retirement but have not confirmed any income figure or date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team AI Plateau still leaves people responsible for a water bill a household can understand. A family cannot drink a software correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel my current wages and Mira’s library pay are steady. Four months saved gives us room to handle a repair bill, though I am still learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing meter entries with the printed bill and have a senior review each fix. I’d continue our 150 monthly savings transfer while both wages arrive. In the first year I’d ask the utility clerk to read any new explanation before it goes to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our work and mortgage in this picture. I do not love every junior task, but no one is threatening my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill showed a human check mattered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer’s meter had a zero added when the reading was typed. The clerk caught it because the bill was ten times larger than the previous month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would keep our usual library and software hours. We would check our actual retirement statements later rather than guess what they will pay.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave humans answerable for water bills.
I would keep **utility-clerk review** of customer explanations.
think: I expect **both wages** to stay steady for now.
Our **four-month reserve** can absorb an ordinary repair bill.
do: **Compare** meter entries with printed bills under senior review.
**Ask** utility clerk to check explanations before release.
feel: **Calm** about work and mortgage while hours hold.
S0.quote: A family cannot drink a software correction.
fieldNote: He uses **meter records and clerks**, not AI, to check a bill’s meaning.
A **four-month cushion** and two regular wages make the mild case secure.

steps.text: Keep checking meter entries and bill explanations with senior and clerk
Transfer 150 monthly to savings while both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write billing code and check routine entries before robots repair pipes. I would ask our union to demand paid review time and a clear person for disputed water bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company may give my small fixes to AI and reduce junior hours. Four months saved buys a pause, not a second career, and I am not quick to learn a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the workplace union’s billing group and bring three cases where the meter number was right but the bill still misled a household. I’d keep my current checks while they are paid. In the first year, if junior hours fall, I’d apply to actual utility support openings only when the stated wage and Mira’s pay cover our mortgage and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours. I can look for another paid role, but I will not resign on a job advert alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One bill showed a leak estimate as water already used. I would bring that to the union because a customer should not have to prove the wording was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mira’s wage cover the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira’s library job helps, but it does not cover the whole mortgage. We would use her usual hours, not overtime the library has not offered.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach billing code before pipe robots.
I would demand **paid human review** for disputed water bills.
think: I expect my **junior hours** could shrink.
I know **four months saved** does not buy a new career.
do: **Join** union billing group with three misleading-bill cases.
**Keep** paid meter and explanation checks while hours remain.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real utility openings with household-covering stated wages.
feel: **Anxious** about my own hours, with some room to search.
S1.quote: I will not resign on a job advert alone.
fieldNote: He joins the **union billing group** with concrete cases of misleading bills.
A **job change** waits for an actual opening whose wage plus Mira’s usual hours covers bills.

steps.text: Join union billing group with three water-bill cases
Keep paid meter checks and clerk-reviewed explanations while hours remain
Apply if hours fall to real utility posts only when combined usual pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do our billing-code work in 2028, with hands-on pipe robots around 2031. Utility customers would still need a fair way to challenge a bill, even if the company removes programmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect junior roles, including mine, to be cut. Four months of savings gives us more time than some neighbours, but it cannot prove a new software wage exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to press as a group for written notice, severance terms and a human bill-appeal route. I’d contact our mortgage lender before missing a payment if laid off and hold our reserve for housing. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help, while Mira keeps her regular library hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage before a new post is ready. I would lie awake over the fourth mortgage payment, not the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children cover your bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children what happened, but not put their pay into our plan. They have rent of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle bill appeals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the utility clerk what happens to an appeal after the code team is gone. A named person must still answer the household, not just close a ticket.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach billing code before 2031 pipe robots.
I would demand **human bill appeals** after coding cuts.
think: I expect **junior cuts** could include me when billing code becomes cheap to produce.
I know **four months saved** cannot guarantee another software wage after full thinking AI.
do: **Organise** union demand for written notice, severance and human appeals.
**Hold** reserve for mortgage and call lender before missed payment if laid off.
**Apply** to actual paid openings and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing my wage before another job exists.
S2.quote: I would lie awake over the fourth mortgage payment, not the first.
fieldNote: He expects **coding loss in 2028**, while physical pipe robots follow around 2031.
His **four-month reserve** buys time, not assurance; union action and eligible help are explicit.

steps.text: Organise union demand for written notice, severance and human water-bill appeals
Apply after 2028 dismissal to real paid openings; contact lender before missed mortgage payment
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 still reaches our software work in 2031 and pipe robots around 2034. Five years lets us test whether a water-customer advocate role is actually staffed and paid, rather than call it a safe haven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my junior code post could end. I would be willing to learn how to hear and document bill disputes, but full thinking AI might also take that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d attend the free evening bill-dispute sessions run by the local tenants’ group, after my paid shift, to practise interviewing and writing case notes. I’d ask the utility for a real advocate vacancy and written wage before applying. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d take that role only if staff still handle appeals and the wage plus Mira’s usual pay covers mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my code wage, with time to learn without paying tuition. The five years matter only if a real employer still hires an advocate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the evening sessions teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the tenants’ group I would listen to a person explain a meter reading before opening the form. I need practice hearing water-bill disputes, not another coding shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mira need more hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira would keep her library hours; I would not ask her to take unoffered overtime. Our four months saved would stay for bills, not course fees.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 pipe robots.
I would test **paid advocate demand** before calling it another career.
think: I expect my **junior post** could end.
I know **bill-appeal work** might also shrink under full thinking AI.
do: **Practise** bill-dispute interviews at free evening tenants’ sessions after paid shifts.
**Ask** utility for real advocate vacancy and written wage.
**Take** role after 2031 only if staff still handle appeals and combined usual wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with free time to learn.
S3.quote: I need practice hearing water-bill disputes, not another coding shortcut.
fieldNote: He learns **dispute interviewing** at free evening sessions without tuition or lost paid hours.
A **real advocate post** must still exist after 2031 and pay enough with Mira’s usual wage.

steps.text: Practise bill-dispute interviews at free evening tenants group after paid shifts
Take actual advocate post after 2031 only if still staffed and combined usual pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 threatens billing code in 2036, with hands-on pipe robots around 2039. A decade should give our union time to demand funded transitions and a real appeals route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my hours are safe this year but junior work may shrink before 2036. Retirement could be possible by then, but we have not verified the figures and I will not assume a pension pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the paid meter checks and continue our 150 monthly savings transfer while both wages arrive. I’d bring the union yearly figures on junior hours and rejected bill appeals. In the first year after 2036, if my job ends, I’d seek actual paid work; I would retire only if verified income and savings cover the mortgage and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a slow loss of junior work, though our present wages and mortgage are stable. Ten years lets us ask for figures instead of making a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement statements with Mira and compare them with the remaining mortgage. A guess from someone else’s pension is not our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the union measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the appeal cases without customer names in our union file. A pattern of rejected cases is more useful than one angry speech.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 pipe robots.
I would demand **funded transitions** and a staffed appeals route.
think: I expect **junior hours** may shrink before 2036.
I cannot assume **pension income** covers our mortgage without verified figures.
do: **Keep** paid meter checks and save 150 monthly while both wages hold.
**Bring** union yearly figures on junior hours and rejected appeals.
**Request written retirement statements** with Mira; after 2036 loss seek paid work, retiring only if verified resources cover mortgage and living costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later junior cuts, with current wages stable.
S4.quote: A guess from someone else’s pension is not our budget.
fieldNote: He keeps **current work** and savings while two regular wages support the mortgage.
The **union file** tracks rejected appeals, while retirement waits on written personal figures.

Save 150 monthly while both wages arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior team could go before we have a proper transition. Written terms, a fair appeal process for customers, eligible income help and real paid openings would help. Four months saved gives us some time, but not a new job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the person paying the water bill whether the explanation makes sense. The meter has a number; the household has to live with the bill.

headlineQuote: The meter has a number; the household has to live with the bill.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and four months saved.
He never uses **AI tools**, checking water bills against meter records, clerks and senior review.
His partner’s **library wage** is regular, giving the household more room than a thin cushion.
He pursues **union demands** and free dispute-interview practice, but changes jobs only for real adequate pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior role before a proper paid transition.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, fair customer appeals, eligible income help and real paid openings would help.
